items.stem: Which term matches this definition: “a community of interacting organisms and their physical environment”?
items.answer: Ecosystem
items.markingKey: Ecosystem: a community of interacting organisms and their physical environment. [1]

items.stem: Explain why energy is lost between trophic levels.
items.answer: Not all the organism is eaten (roots, bones); not all eaten material is digested (lost in faeces); energy is used in respiration and lost as heat; energy is used for movement.
items.markingKey: 1 mark per reason up to [3]

items.stem: Explain why the open ocean has low productivity per square metre even though it covers a large area.
items.answer: Nutrients are scarce in surface waters because dead material sinks; light penetrates only the upper layers, so phytoplankton growth is limited except in upwelling zones.
items.markingKey: nutrient shortage [1]; light limited with depth [1] [2]

items.stem: A student studied a freshwater pond food web: algae and pondweed → water fleas and snails → small fish and dragonfly larvae → herons. Suggest how a pollutant could reach high concentrations in the top predator.
items.answer: A persistent pollutant (e.g. mercury, DDT) is not broken down or excreted; it accumulates in each organism and is concentrated up the food chain (biomagnification).

items.stem: Fig. 4.1 shows a food web for a mangrove ecosystem in Indonesia: mangrove leaves and algae are eaten by crabs, snails and small fish; these are eaten by larger fish and wading birds; crocodiles and sea eagles are top predators. (a) Draw a food chain with four organisms from the food web. (b) Explain why there are fewer top predators than primary consumers.
items.answer: (a) e.g. algae → snail → small fish → heron (or mangrove leaves → crab → larger fish → sea eagle). (b) Energy is lost at each trophic level, so less energy is available to support top predators.

items.stem: Fig. 4.1 shows a food web for a mangrove ecosystem in Vietnam’s Mekong Delta: mangrove leaves and algae are eaten by crabs, snails and small fish; these are eaten by larger fish and wading birds; crocodiles and sea eagles are top predators. (a) Draw a food chain with four organisms from the food web. (b) Suggest the effect on the food web if one primary consumer were removed.
items.answer: (a) e.g. algae → snail → small fish → heron (or mangrove leaves → crab → larger fish → sea eagle). (b) Its food (producers) would increase; its predators would decline or switch to other prey, increasing pressure on other primary consumers.
items.markingKey: (a) [1] (b) 1 mark per developed effect up to [3]

items.stem: Which term matches this definition: “the position an organism occupies in a food chain, such as producer or primary consumer”?
items.answer: Trophic level
items.markingKey: Trophic level: the position an organism occupies in a food chain, such as producer or primary consumer. [1]

items.stem: A student writes: “Most of the energy from the Sun that reaches a leaf is converted into plant biomass.” Is this statement correct? Explain your answer.
items.answer: Not correct. Only about 1-3% is fixed by photosynthesis; the rest is reflected, transmitted or not absorbed by chlorophyll.
items.markingKey: 1 mark correct judgement; 1 mark accurate explanation [2]

items.stem: Which term matches this definition: “the conversion of nitrogen gas into ammonia or nitrates, by bacteria such as Rhizobium, by lightning or by the Haber process”?
items.answer: Nitrogen fixation
items.markingKey: Nitrogen fixation: the conversion of nitrogen gas into ammonia or nitrates, by bacteria such as Rhizobium, by lightning or by the Haber process. [1]

items.stem: Describe how carbon is transferred from the atmosphere to the soil.
items.answer: Plants absorb CO₂ in photosynthesis and build organic compounds; leaves, roots and dead plants (and animals that ate them) fall to the ground; decomposers incorporate part of the carbon into humus.
items.markingKey: photosynthesis [1]; death / litter fall [1]; decomposition to humus [1] [3]

items.stem: Explain how human activities have altered the carbon cycle.
items.answer: Burning fossil fuels transfers carbon from long-term stores to the atmosphere; deforestation reduces photosynthesis and releases carbon from biomass and soils; cement production releases CO₂; farming disturbs soil carbon.
items.markingKey: 1 mark per developed point up to [3]

items.stem: Fig. 4.2 shows a simplified nitrogen cycle for a farm in Nairobi, with fertiliser input, legumes, livestock manure, crops harvested and nitrate leaching into a stream. Explain the role of legumes in the nitrogen cycle on the farm.
items.answer: Nitrogen-fixing bacteria in their root nodules convert N₂ into ammonium, adding nitrogen to the soil and reducing fertiliser needs.

items.stem: Fig. 4.2 shows a simplified nitrogen cycle for a farm in Auckland, with fertiliser input, legumes, livestock manure, crops harvested and nitrate leaching into a stream. (a) Name the process by which bacteria convert ammonium in manure to nitrate. (b) Explain the role of legumes in the nitrogen cycle on the farm.
items.answer: (a) Nitrification (b) Nitrogen-fixing bacteria in their root nodules convert N₂ into ammonium, adding nitrogen to the soil and reducing fertiliser needs.

items.stem: Fig. 4.2 shows a simplified nitrogen cycle for a farm in Manila, with fertiliser input, legumes, livestock manure, crops harvested and nitrate leaching into a stream. (a) Explain why nitrate is easily lost from the soil. (b) Explain the role of legumes in the nitrogen cycle on the farm.
items.answer: (a) Nitrate ions are very soluble and are not held by negatively charged soil particles, so they are washed out by drainage water (leaching). (b) Nitrogen-fixing bacteria in their root nodules convert N₂ into ammonium, adding nitrogen to the soil and reducing fertiliser needs.

items.stem: A farm applies 180 kg of nitrogen fertiliser per hectare each year to wheat. Measurements show high nitrate concentrations in a stream draining the farm. (a) Explain why nitrate is easily lost from the soil. (b) Explain the role of legumes in the nitrogen cycle on the farm.
items.answer: (a) Nitrate ions are very soluble and are not held by negatively charged soil particles, so they are washed out by drainage water (leaching). (b) Nitrogen-fixing bacteria in their root nodules convert N₂ into ammonium, adding nitrogen to the soil and reducing fertiliser needs.

items.stem: Fig. 4.2 shows a simplified nitrogen cycle for a farm in Toronto, with fertiliser input, legumes, livestock manure, crops harvested and nitrate leaching into a stream. (a) Explain why nitrate is easily lost from the soil. (b) Describe the possible effects of the leached nitrate on the stream.
items.answer: (a) Nitrate ions are very soluble and are not held by negatively charged soil particles, so they are washed out by drainage water (leaching). (b) Eutrophication: algal blooms, death of plants, oxygen depletion by bacteria, fish deaths; drinking water may exceed safe nitrate limits.
items.markingKey: (a) [2] (b) 1 mark per effect up to [3]

items.stem: Which term matches this definition: “the conversion of nitrogen gas into ammonia or nitrates, by bacteria such as Rhizobium, by lightning or by the Haber process”?
items.answer: Nitrogen fixation
items.markingKey: Nitrogen fixation: the conversion of nitrogen gas into ammonia or nitrates, by bacteria such as Rhizobium, by lightning or by the Haber process. [1]

items.stem: Explain how the use of nitrogen fertilisers affects the nitrogen cycle.
items.answer: The Haber process fixes very large amounts of atmospheric nitrogen; excess nitrate leaches into rivers causing eutrophication; denitrification releases nitrous oxide, a greenhouse gas.
items.markingKey: 1 mark per point up to [3]

items.stem: Estimated global carbon fluxes (Gt C per year): fossil fuels and cement 9.9; land-use change 1.2; uptake by the ocean 2.8; uptake by land vegetation 3.1. The atmosphere stores about 875 Gt C. 1 ppm of CO₂ ≈ 2.12 Gt C. (a) Convert the annual increase into ppm of CO₂. (b) Suggest one reason why the land sink may weaken in future.
items.answer: (a) 2.45 ppm per year (b) Deforestation, drought, wildfires and higher temperatures increase respiration and decomposition, releasing stored carbon.

items.stem: “Human activities have changed the nitrogen cycle more than the carbon cycle.” Discuss.
items.answer: For: The Haber process and legume crops now fix more nitrogen than all natural land processes combined, roughly doubling nitrogen inputs; this causes eutrophication, dead zones (Gulf of Mexico) and N₂O emissions. Against: Fossil-fuel burning and deforestation have increased atmospheric CO₂ by about 50%, causing climate change and ocean acidification with global consequences. Judgement: Proportionally the nitrogen cycle has been changed more, but changes to the carbon cycle have the greatest global impact.
items.markingKey: Indicative content as in the model answer. Level 4 (10-12 marks): detailed, balanced evaluation supported by named examples and a clear, justified conclusion. Level 3 (7-9 marks): developed discussion with examples, judgement partly supported. Level 2 (4-6 marks): some relevant points, mostly descriptive. Level 1 (1-3 marks): simple, unsupported statements. [12]

items.stem: Which term matches this definition: “a large global ecosystem defined by its climate and dominant vegetation, such as tropical rainforest or tundra”?
items.answer: Biome
items.markingKey: Biome: a large global ecosystem defined by its climate and dominant vegetation, such as tropical rainforest or tundra. [1]

items.stem: Explain why tropical rainforests have high biodiversity.
items.answer: High temperatures and rainfall all year give high productivity; a stable climate over long periods allowed many species to evolve; layered structure provides many niches.
items.markingKey: 1 mark per developed reason up to [3]

items.stem: Describe the changes that take place during primary succession on bare rock.
items.answer: Pioneer lichens and mosses colonise and weather the rock; they die and add organic matter, forming thin soil; grasses and herbs grow, then shrubs and finally trees; soil deepens, biodiversity and biomass increase until a climax community forms.
items.markingKey: 1 mark per stage up to [4]

items.stem: Fig. 4.3 shows a transect across sand dunes at a coastal site, from embryo dunes near the sea to woodland 400 m inland. Species number, soil organic matter and pH were recorded every 50 m. Suggest why soil pH falls with distance inland.
items.answer: Shell fragments (calcium carbonate) are leached and humus from plants adds organic acids.

items.stem: Students in Mumbai studied succession on a sand dune system. Near the sea only marram grass and sea couch grew; 300 m inland there was heath and woodland with over 20 species. (a) Suggest why soil pH falls with distance inland. (b) Suggest how trampling by tourists could affect the succession.
items.answer: (a) Shell fragments (calcium carbonate) are leached and humus from plants adds organic acids. (b) It destroys vegetation and exposes sand to wind erosion (blowouts), setting succession back.

items.stem: Students in Lima studied succession on a sand dune system. Near the sea only marram grass and sea couch grew; 300 m inland there was heath and woodland with over 20 species. (a) Explain why marram grass is able to grow on the young dunes. (b) Suggest how trampling by tourists could affect the succession.
items.answer: (a) It tolerates burial, salt spray and drought; it has long roots to reach water and grows upward when buried. (b) It destroys vegetation and exposes sand to wind erosion (blowouts), setting succession back.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark per adaptation up to [2] (b) [2]

items.stem: Explain why biodiversity is important.
items.answer: It provides food, medicines and materials; ecosystem services such as pollination, water purification and climate regulation; resilience of ecosystems; cultural and aesthetic value; intrinsic value.
items.markingKey: 1 mark per point up to [3]

Which term matches this definition: “protecting species in their natural habitats, for example in national parks and nature reserves”?
items.answer: In situ conservation
items.markingKey: In situ conservation: protecting species in their natural habitats, for example in national parks and nature reserves. [1]

items.stem: Explain how habitat fragmentation threatens species.
items.answer: Small patches support only small populations; edges change conditions; animals cannot move to find mates or food; inbreeding reduces genetic diversity; populations are vulnerable to local extinction.
items.markingKey: 1 mark per point up to [3]

items.stem: Explain the advantages of in situ conservation compared with ex situ conservation.
items.answer: Species stay in their natural habitat with natural behaviour, food and interactions; whole ecosystems and many species are protected together; evolution continues; usually cheaper per species.
items.markingKey: 1 mark per advantage up to [3]

items.stem: Refer to your case study of a conservation project (for example the Amazon rainforest, Brazil). Briefly describe the threats to biodiversity.
items.answer: the Amazon rainforest, Brazil: Cattle ranching, soya farming, logging, mining and road building; about 17% of the forest has been lost; fires; climate change may cause dieback.
items.markingKey: 1 mark named, located example; up to 3 marks for accurate, place-specific points. named threats with explanation and data [4]

items.stem: The original forest area of Borneo was about 740 000 km². About 17% has been cleared, and current clearance is about 1 500 km² per year. (a) Calculate the area of forest remaining. (b) Calculate the annual clearance as a percentage of the remaining forest. (c) Suggest two strategies to reduce the rate of deforestation.
items.answer: (a) 614 200 km² (b) 0.24% (c) Protected areas and indigenous land rights with enforcement; satellite monitoring; certification (FSC, RSPO) and supply-chain bans; payments for ecosystem services (REDD+).

items.stem: Name an example of a conservation project. For your chosen example, describe the threats to biodiversity.
items.answer: Model answer (the Galápagos Islands, Ecuador): Invasive goats, rats and plants; overfishing; tourism growth (over 250 000 visitors a year); climate change and El Niño affecting marine food supply.
items.markingKey: Indicative content: named threats with explanation and data Level 3 (5-6 marks): well-developed points on both sides with examples and a supported conclusion. Level 2 (3-4 marks): some developed points, limited balance or example. Level 1 (1-2 marks): simple statements. [6]

items.stem: With reference to the Kew Millennium Seed Bank, UK, or another example of a conservation project, evaluate the effectiveness of the conservation strategies used.
items.answer: Model answer (the Kew Millennium Seed Bank, UK): Stores seeds of over 40 000 species from more than 190 countries at −20 °C; partners worldwide; seeds used for research and to restore habitats, but seeds of some species (e.g. many tropical trees) cannot be stored.
items.markingKey: Indicative content: in situ / ex situ methods, evidence of success, limitations, judgement Level 3 (6-8 marks): detailed, balanced discussion using place-specific detail from the named example and data, with a reasoned judgement. items.stem: A student writes: “Zoos are the best way to conserve endangered species.” Is this statement correct? Explain your answer.
items.answer: Not correct. Zoos can support captive breeding and education, but they hold small populations and cannot conserve whole ecosystems; in situ protection is usually more effective.
items.markingKey: 1 mark correct judgement; 1 mark accurate explanation [2]

items.stem: The original forest area of Sumatra was about 480 000 km². About 15% has been cleared, and current clearance is about 5 000 km² per year. Explain two impacts of the deforestation on biodiversity.
items.answer: Habitat loss leads to population decline and extinction of endemic species; fragmentation isolates populations; edge effects; loss of food sources for dependent species.
items.markingKey: 1 mark each impact with explanation [2]

items.stem: Explain why eating lower in the food chain can feed more people.
items.answer: Energy is lost at each trophic level, so crops eaten directly provide about ten times more energy per hectare than meat from animals fed on crops.
items.markingKey: energy loss per level [1]; more food energy per area [1] [2]

items.stem: In a coral reef, energy flow (kJ/m²/year) at each trophic level was measured: producers 25 000, primary consumers 3 370, secondary consumers 312. Calculate the efficiency of energy transfer from producers to primary consumers.
“Energy flow, not nutrient cycling, limits the size of ecosystems.” Discuss.
items.answer: For: Energy is lost as heat at each trophic level, limiting food chain length and the biomass of top predators. Against: Nutrients (nitrogen, phosphorus) often limit productivity, e.g. in the open ocean or tropical rainforest soils; water and temperature also limit NPP. Judgement: Energy flow limits food chain length, but nutrients, water and temperature often limit the productivity of the producers.

items.stem: A student writes: “Planting forests can help to reduce atmospheric carbon dioxide.” Is this statement correct? Explain your answer.
items.answer: Correct. Growing trees remove CO₂ by photosynthesis and store carbon in wood and soil, though the store can be lost by fire or felling.
items.markingKey: 1 mark correct judgement; 1 mark accurate explanation [2]

items.stem: Explain why ocean acidification is linked to the carbon cycle.
items.answer: Oceans absorb CO₂ from the atmosphere; it dissolves to form carbonic acid, lowering pH and reducing carbonate ions that corals and shellfish need to build shells and skeletons.
items.markingKey: CO₂ absorbed [1]; carbonic acid / lower pH [1]; effect on organisms [1] [3]

Suggest two ways the farmer could increase the percentage taken up by the crop.
items.answer: Split applications timed to crop growth; precision application using soil tests; slow-release fertilisers; avoid application before rain; improve soil organic matter.
items.markingKey: 1 mark each [2]

items.stem: What is meant by the term “biome”?
options: The variety of life in an area, including genetic, species and ecosystem (habitat) diversity.
A large global ecosystem defined by its climate and dominant vegetation, such as tropical rainforest or tundra.
The number of different species in an area.
How similar the population sizes of the different species in an area are.

items.answer: Human activities such as grazing, burning, mowing or felling keep the community at an earlier stage (a plagioclimax), e.g. heather moorland maintained by burning.

items.stem: “The main value of biodiversity is economic.” Discuss. In your answer you should consider: intrinsic value; ecosystem services; medicines.
items.answer: For: Biodiversity provides food, timber, medicines (about 25% of drugs come from plants), tourism income and ecosystem services worth trillions of dollars a year. Against: It also has ecological value (resilience, stability), cultural and spiritual value, and intrinsic value; many species have no known economic use. Judgement: Economic value is a powerful argument for conservation, but biodiversity also has ecological and ethical value that cannot be measured in money.

items.stem: In a class discussion, a student says: “Climate change is becoming a major threat to biodiversity.” Is this statement correct? Explain your answer.

Felix argues that in situ conservation is more effective than ex situ conservation. Discuss this view, referring to named examples. In your answer you should consider: costs; named examples; reintroduction.
items.answer: For: Protecting habitats conserves whole ecosystems, natural behaviour and evolution (e.g. Galápagos, Serengeti); it is cheaper per species. Against: Ex situ methods are vital when habitats are destroyed or populations are tiny: the Arabian oryx and California condor were saved by captive breeding; seed banks store huge genetic diversity. Judgement: The two are complementary: in situ is generally more effective, but ex situ provides an insurance policy and supports reintroductions.

(a) Name the process by which bacteria convert ammonium in manure to nitrate. (b) Explain why nitrate is easily lost from the soil. (c) Explain the role of legumes in the nitrogen cycle on the farm.
items.answer: (a) Nitrification (b) Nitrate ions are very soluble and are not held by negatively charged soil particles, so they are washed out by drainage water (leaching). (c) Nitrogen-fixing bacteria in their root nodules convert N₂ into ammonium, adding nitrogen to the soil and reducing fertiliser needs.

items.stem: What is meant by the term “biodiversity”?
options: How similar the population sizes of the different species in an area are.
The number of different species in an area.
The variety of life in an area, including genetic, species and ecosystem (habitat) diversity.
The gradual change in the species of a community over time.
items.answer: The variety of life in an area, including genetic, species and ecosystem (habitat) diversity.
items.markingKey: Biodiversity: the variety of life in an area, including genetic, species and ecosystem (habitat) diversity. [1]

items.stem: A student writes: “Biodiversity always increases steadily throughout succession.” Is this statement correct? Explain your answer.
items.answer: Not correct. It usually increases through the middle stages but may fall slightly at the climax when a few dominant species (e.g. trees) shade out others.
items.markingKey: 1 mark correct judgement; 1 mark accurate explanation [2]

items.stem: Students in Accra studied succession on a sand dune system. Near the sea only marram grass and sea couch grew; 300 m inland there was heath and woodland with over 20 species. Suggest how trampling by tourists could affect the succession.
items.answer: It destroys vegetation and exposes sand to wind erosion (blowouts), setting succession back.

items.stem: Students in Mexico City studied succession on a sand dune system. Near the sea only marram grass and sea couch grew; 300 m inland there was heath and woodland with over 20 species. (a) Describe how the number of species changes with distance from the sea. (b) Explain why marram grass is able to grow on the young dunes. (c) Suggest why soil pH falls with distance inland. (d) Suggest how trampling by tourists could affect the succession.
items.answer: (a) It increases inland from very few on embryo dunes to many in fixed dunes and woodland. (b) It tolerates burial, salt spray and drought; it has long roots to reach water and grows upward when buried. (c) Shell fragments (calcium carbonate) are leached and humus from plants adds organic acids. (d) It destroys vegetation and exposes sand to wind erosion (blowouts), setting succession back.
items.markingKey: (a) [2] (b) 1 mark per adaptation up to [2] (c) [2] (d) [2]

items.stem: A news article states: “Protected areas always stop biodiversity loss.” Is this statement correct? Explain your answer.
items.answer: Not correct. Some are “paper parks” with weak enforcement, are too small, or are affected by pollution, climate change and invasive species.
items.markingKey: 1 mark correct judgement; 1 mark accurate explanation [2]

items.stem: Explain why the illegal wildlife trade threatens species such as rhinos and pangolins.
items.answer: High prices for horn and scales (used in traditional medicine or as status items) encourage poaching; slow-breeding species cannot replace losses; poverty and weak enforcement make poaching attractive.
items.markingKey: 1 mark per point up to [3]

items.stem: The wild population of the greater one-horned rhino in India and Nepal was estimated at 1 500 in 1985 and 4 014 in 2021. Calculate the percentage change in the population.

The original forest area of Borneo was about 740 000 km². About 25% has been cleared, and current clearance is about 3 500 km² per year. Scientists suggest a tipping point if a further quarter of the remaining forest is lost. Estimate how many years this would take at the current rate.
items.answer: 39.6 years

items.stem: The original forest area of the Congo Basin was about 1 700 000 km². About 15% has been cleared, and current clearance is about 1 500 km² per year. (a) Calculate the annual clearance as a percentage of the remaining forest. (b) Suggest two strategies to reduce the rate of deforestation.
items.answer: (a) 0.10% (b) Protected areas and indigenous land rights with enforcement; satellite monitoring; certification (FSC, RSPO) and supply-chain bans; payments for ecosystem services (REDD+).

items.stem: Evaluate the view that habitat loss is a greater threat to biodiversity than climate change. In your answer you should consider: deforestation; interactions between threats; coral reefs.
items.answer: For: Land-use change is currently the leading cause of species decline (IPBES), e.g. palm oil in Borneo and cattle ranching in the Amazon. Against: Climate change is accelerating: coral bleaching on the Great Barrier Reef, range shifts and predicted extinctions; it interacts with other threats. Judgement: Habitat loss is the main threat now, but climate change may become as important later this century.
items.markingKey: Indicative content as in the model answer. Level 3 (11-15 marks): good knowledge and examples, some evaluation, conclusion partly supported. Level 2 (6-10 marks): relevant but mainly descriptive, limited examples or one-sided. Level 1 (1-5 marks): a few simple, generalised points with little or no evaluation. [20]
